title: TBX Home Broadcast Station
description: A home television broadcast station on a Raspberry Pi 5, built out of a media collecting habit. Numbered channels, a real schedule, and a seek algorithm that drops you into whatever is playing right now rather than starting a file from the beginning. FastAPI and mpv over a Unix socket, and a React UI driven by an IR remote.

steps.title: What It Is
steps.text:
A broadcast station, not a media server. The distinction is the schedule. A media server hands you a library and waits for you to pick something; TBX decides what is on and you tune to it.
It came out of collecting media as a hobby. Past a certain size a collection stops being something you browse - there is too much of it to pick from, and scrolling a grid of everything you own is a worse experience than having something already playing. TBX is what to do with a collection once it has got to that point.
It runs on a Raspberry Pi 5 with 16GB of RAM and boots straight to playback. A FastAPI backend drives an mpv playback engine over a Unix socket. The web UI is React, and the whole thing is operated with a handheld IR remote. Holding T drops out of playback into a kiosk mode for managing the media directly, so adding and organizing the collection does not mean going to a terminal.
Built solo over about two years.
steps.alt: TBX web UI showing the channel grid and now-playing display

steps.title: The Seek Problem
steps.text:
The hard part of making something behave like a broadcast network is that there is no play button. If you tune to Channel 4 at 8:00 on a Tuesday, the right thing to do is join whatever is airing, partway through, exactly where it would be.
So a channel is not a playlist with a cursor. It is a schedule plus a clock. On every tune the backend resolves the current wall time against the channel's schedule, works out which item is airing and how far into it the moment falls, and seeks mpv to that offset. Nothing is stored about where a viewer left off, because a real channel does not care - it runs whether anyone is watching or not.
Two viewers tuning to the same channel see the same frame.

steps.title: The Interface
steps.text:
The target was that normal use never involves a keyboard - you tune, you watch, and the kiosk mode is there when you actually want to manage the collection.
Color palette is dark, amber, and gunmetal, which is what the analog broadcast gear it is imitating actually looked like.

steps.title: Channel 99
steps.text:
Channel 99 is a hidden game console rather than a channel. Two original games are in progress for it, sharing one setting and one continuity rather than being unrelated one-offs.
This is the part of the project furthest from finished, and it is deliberately last - the station has to work as a station before the easter egg matters.

steps.title: Where It Is Now
steps.text:
v1 is built and living in an enclosure. It runs, it holds a schedule, and you operate it with the remote like any other box under a television.
It is a v1, so it is not finished - but it is past the stage of being parts on a desk, and it earns its shelf.

title: Blu - A Compiled Programming Language
alt: Blu - a compiled programming language written from scratch, targeting x86-64 Linux
description: A compiled programming language built from scratch, for no reason other than finding out whether I could. Full pipeline from lexer to native x86-64 codegen, running on Linux, with closures, record types inferred from usage, a standard library, and 400+ regression tests that have to stay green.

steps.title: Why
steps.text:
No practical reason. I wanted to find out whether I could build a real one - not a toy interpreter, but something with a full pipeline that emits native code and can be held to the same standards as a tool you would actually use.
Blu compiles to native x86-64 assembly and runs on Linux. The compiler is written in C++.

steps.title: The Pipeline
steps.text:
Five stages: lexer, parser, semantic analyzer, IR, x86-64 codegen.
The order they were built in matters. Lexer first, made deterministic before anything depended on it. Parser next. Then semantic analysis - undefined variables, wrong argument counts, duplicate declarations - which is the layer nobody notices until it is missing and errors start surfacing as bad codegen instead of as compile errors.

steps.title: Language Design
steps.text:
Semantics were frozen early, before the standard library went in, so the language could not drift while it was being built on.
Records are called forms, and their field types are inferred from usage across the call graph rather than declared. The keywords are give for return, show for print, and when for if.
The standard library covers JSON, CSV, binary encoding, key-value arrays used as databases, process spawning, and environment variables.

steps.title: Regression Infrastructure
steps.text:
The test suite is the thing keeping the project honest. Several hundred regression tests organized by category, run by shell scripts that report pass rates, now past 400.
The rule is that nothing lands until every test is green. On a compiler this is not optional - a change to codegen can silently break a language feature three layers away, and without the suite you find out weeks later in a program that used to work.

steps.title: Closures, and a Build That Would Not Link
steps.text:
Closures and forms went in together. Closures meant environment objects, closure allocation, and a new family of IR instructions to capture variables across stack frames. Forms meant inferring field types from how they were used across the whole call graph.
Partway in, the build collapsed into a cascade of errors that pointed everywhere and nowhere. The cause was not in the new code: #include directives had been placed after the opening brace of namespace blu, so the entire standard library had been pulled inside the namespace. Every symbol resolved to the wrong place.
By the time it was found, ir_builder.cpp had accumulated duplicate function bodies and orphaned copy-paste blocks from working around symptoms of it. Rewriting the file from scratch was faster than untangling it. Each fix exposed the next one; individually all of them were small.
Forms edge cases finished at 113/113, closure regression at 10/10.

steps.title: File I/O
steps.text:
Blu could not touch the filesystem, which put a ceiling on what could be written in it. file.read, file.write, file.append, and file.exists: four C symbols, four arity checks, four codegen entries.
The verification program wrote a file, read it back, and confirmed it existed - which is the first point at which a Blu program could do something that outlived its own process.

steps.title: What Is Left
steps.text:
Plenty. A map type, a garbage collector, line numbers in error messages, a formatter, a REPL, a module system, a C FFI bridge, and a platform layer.
It compiles and the tests pass, which is a long way from done.
